title: No cheating
hook: Nanak weighed grain honestly at Sultanpur
tomorrow: Simran posts 'today's seva: my shift'. can a paid job be seva?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lalo's plain bread and a fake-review offer turned down: clean work. Week two at the stall brings a smaller test.

The stall's old hanging scale reads a little heavy. Hang nothing on it, and the needle still sits past zero. So every bag of plums weighs a bit more than it is. Mrs. Ortega, who owns the stall, hasn't noticed. Simran has. And she remembers an odd story Bebe once told her, about Guru Nanak weighing grain, and getting stuck on one number. Why would anyone get stuck on a number?
screen: `THE NEEDLE SITS PAST ZERO.` → `EVERY BAG A LITTLE HEAVY.` → `STUCK ON ONE NUMBER?`

segments.voice: Here's the story, as tradition tells it. As a young man, Nanak worked as a storekeeper at Sultanpur, weighing out grain and counting each measure aloud in Punjabi. One, two, three. When he reached thirteen, the word was tera. And tera also means yours. So, the story goes, he kept weighing and kept saying tera, tera: yours, yours, God's, and couldn't move past it. Someone complained that he was giving the stores away. When the stock was checked, tradition says, nothing was missing. That's the puzzle solved. The count stalled because one word did two jobs at once. Every measure Nanak handed over, he heard: this is yours, not mine. And when the measure belongs to God, you don't shave it. The Granth talks about trade the same way. On ang 595, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: make your passing days the shop, and make the true Name your goods. A shop like that is always open to inspection. So Simran's fix is not dramatic at all. She finds the small screw at the top of the scale, turns it until the needle rests on zero, and tells Mrs. Ortega why. Mrs. Ortega squints at it, then laughs: how long has it been doing that?
screen: `SULTANPUR: WEIGHING OUT GRAIN.` · `TERA: THIRTEEN, AND YOURS.` · `ANG 595: YOUR DAYS ARE THE SHOP.` · `A SCREW TURNED BACK TO ZERO.` · then, large: `FAIR WEIGHTS.`

segments.voice: Pour a glass of water, or measure out a spoonful of something, as exactly as you can: right to the line, not over, not under. Then set it down and sit, with the feeling of a measure that's simply true.
No cheating. Fair weights and honest measures, because what you hand over isn't yours to shave.
Your line: fair weights. Tera, tera: each measure handed over is yours, not mine. Talk tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the Sultanpur 'tera' story to children and in gurdwara talks; in daily trade it stands for exact weights and honest measures.

fork.setup: at your job, the time clock rounds everyone up to the next quarter-hour, in your favor. what does 'fair weights' say?
options: say something; an honest measure doesn't tilt your way either.
keep quiet; the mistake is the company's, not yours.
only bring it up if it ever starts rounding against you.
fork.reveal: Simran fixed a scale that tilted toward the stall. tera: the measure isn't yours to shave, either direction.

original.note: Gurmukhi: tera, yours; in the Sultanpur story, also the count of thirteen.

chat.meaning: Nanak heard 'tera, yours' in every measure. Fair weights means an exact measure, even when nobody would notice.

Sultanpur.meaning: the town where the young Nanak worked as a storekeeper

tera.meaning: yours; in the story, also thirteen
